Let \(A,B,C\) be three consecutive vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon with integer coordinates. Then the vectors

\[
u=B-A,\qquad v=C-B
\]

are integer vectors of equal length. The angle between consecutive side vectors is exactly the exterior angle

\[
\theta=\frac{2\pi}{n}.
\]

Thus

\[
\cos\theta=\frac{u\cdot v}{\|u\|^2}\in \mathbb Q,\qquad 
\sin\theta=\frac{\det(u,v)}{\|u\|^2}\in \mathbb Q.
\]

So \(\sin(2\pi/n)\) and \(\cos(2\pi/n)\) are both rational. Since \((2\pi/n)/\pi=2/n\) is rational, Niven’s theorem applies: if \(\sin\theta\) is rational and \(\theta/\pi\) is rational, then

\[
\sin\theta\in \left\{0,\pm \frac12,\pm 1\right\}.
\]

Checking \(n\ge 3\) with both sine and cosine rational, the only possibility is

\[
\theta=\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2},
\]

so \(n=4\). A square with integer vertices exists, for example \((0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)\).

Therefore the only integer is

\[
\boxed{4}.
\]
